descriptionChirho: A whip or scourge used as an instrument of physical punishment. Used of the Roman examination by scourging in Acts 22:24 (mastixin, 'that he should be examined with whips') and of the sufferings of OT saints who endured mockings and scourgings in Heb 11:36 (mastigon, 'of scourgings'). The multilingual glosses reflect the concrete instrument: Arabic bi-l-siyat (with whips)/jaldat (lashes), Hebrew be-shotim (with whips)/malqot (beatings/lashes), Korean chaejjig-euro (with a whip)/chaejjig-deul-eui (of whips), Spanish con azotes/azotes, Hindi kodon se (with whips), German Geisseln (scourges), French fleau (scourge).

A disease, affliction, or plague conceived figuratively as a 'scourge' or 'lash' from God. Used of the woman healed from her flow of blood (Mark 5:29, 5:34 mastigos, 'she was healed of her affliction'), of Jesus healing many of diseases and afflictions (Mark 3:10 mastigas, Luke 7:21 mastigon). The multilingual glosses clearly distinguish this figurative medical sense: Arabic amrad/al-da' (diseases/illness), Hebrew nega/negiot/makkot (plague/affliction/blow), Korean jilbyeong/byeong (disease/sickness), Spanish enfermedad/enfermedades (disease), German Geisseln (used broadly). The semantic shift from 'whip' to 'affliction/plague' follows the common metaphorical extension of striking instruments to divine punishment or disease in Semitic and Greek thought.
